basis: Lilly war/honour judgment: Rupert, as a person of eminency, is signified by the tenth house and its lord the Sun — the Sun peregrine and in his detriment in a fixed sign = a significator with no essential dignity, fixed in a losing condition, incapable of honour from this war. Essex is signified by Venus, lady of the opposite house, and Venus is in reception with Saturn and — decisively — she disposes of Rupert's significator: the opponent's significator disposing of the quesited's means Essex holds the disposition of Rupert's actions and will have the better of him (as at Edgehill, where Essex already kept the ground, a given fact the judgment is calibrated against). Venus also casts a dexter aspect to the cusp of the tenth (Rupert's honour-house) while the Moon casts her sinister aspect to the same cusp = the honour of the tenth is struck from both sides by the opponent and the common course of events. No dignity or reception rescues the Sun. Verdict: no honour, worsting by Essex, and an end in disgrace/withdrawal from the English wars.
prediction_text: Prince Rupert will get no honour by these wars and will be worsted by the Earl of Essex. His significator the Sun is peregrine and in his detriment in a fixed sign, and is disposed of by Essex's significatrix Venus (who is in reception with Saturn and aspects his tenth cusp), so Essex holds the advantage over him; Rupert's part ends in loss of reputation — defeat, disgrace and eventual withdrawal from the war in England — rather than in honour.
timing: Year scale (course of the war, figure c. Nov–Dec 1642): window is the ensuing campaigns; main coordinate is progressive — no single dated battle is asserted from the stated positions, the worsting accumulates over the following war years
